Fourth, report the scam through the official channels below. Keep every reference number you're given.
Reporting a cruise scam in the UK

Report a cruise scam to the police's national fraud service and to the relevant platforms so action can be taken and patterns tracked. In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, report to Report Fraud (the current service, formerly known as Action Fraud) at reportfraud.police.uk or on 0300 123 2040. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland by calling 101. Give as much detail as you can: the company name, website, phone numbers, email addresses, the cruise line or sailing claimed, dates of contact, how you paid and how much you lost. If a scam reached you by text message, forward it free of charge to 7726 so your mobile network can investigate. If you came across a fake or suspicious cruise website, report it to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) through its report-a-scam-website service. You can also report the advert or profile to the platform where you saw it — the social network, marketplace or search engine — so it can be taken down. If you need free, independent advice on your consumer rights or a payment dispute, contact Citizens Advice on 0808 223 1133.
faq: Are all cruises ATOL protected?

No. ATOL is the Civil Aviation Authority's protection scheme and it generally covers flight-inclusive package holidays. A fly-cruise that includes your flights is usually ATOL-protected, but a cruise-only or non-flight booking is not covered by ATOL — it may instead have protection through a bond, insurance, trust arrangement or another scheme, but protection is not automatic for every booking. Don't assume a cruise is ATOL-protected just because it's a big holiday: ask the seller in writing exactly what protection your specific booking carries, and confirm it before you pay.
The cruise seller isn't an ABTA member — does that mean it's a scam?

Not on its own. ABTA membership can be a useful sign of an established travel business, but it is voluntary, and many legitimate companies are not ABTA members. A company not being in ABTA doesn't prove it's fraudulent — and a company displaying an ABTA logo isn't automatically genuine either, since logos can be copied. Treat ABTA membership as one check among several: verify any claimed membership directly with ABTA, look up the company on Companies House, and confirm what financial protection your booking has.
I got a call saying I've won a free cruise — is it real?

Be very cautious. A genuine prize never requires you to pay a fee, "taxes" or "port charges", make a premium-rate call, or hand over card details to claim it. "Free cruise" prize scams use exactly those demands to take your money or your details. If you didn't enter a competition you have almost certainly not won anything. Don't pay, don't share card or personal details, and if you can, report it — forward a scam text to 7726, and report a call or email to Report Fraud (in Scotland, Police Scotland on 101).
I've paid a deposit for a cruise that turned out to be fake — can I get my money back?

It depends on how you paid and how fast you act. If you paid by credit card, ask your provider about a Section 75 claim (a qualifying credit-card purchase over £100 and no more than £30,000). If you paid by debit card, ask about a chargeback. If you paid by UK bank transfer on or after 7 October 2024, mandatory APP fraud reimbursement rules may apply — ask your bank to assess the claim, within the 13-month window. Report the scam to Report Fraud (or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland) and keep all your evidence and reference numbers.
How can I tell a fake cruise booking website from the real one?

Don't reach the site by clicking an ad, email or text link — type the cruise line's or agent's address yourself, or use a trusted search result, and check the full domain carefully, as clone sites copy the branding but use a slightly different web address. Look for verifiable UK company details you can cross-check on Companies House, a genuine landline, and clear answers about which line operates the sailing and what protection applies. If a site pushes you to pay by bank transfer or reroutes you away from a card payment, don't enter your details — report it to the NCSC's report-a-scam-website service.

title: PayPal Friends and Family Scam: Why Sellers Ask for It
excerpt: Scammers pose as friends or sellers to trick you into sending money via PayPal's Friends and Family option, which has no buyer protection.
description: PayPal Friends and Family payments are not eligible for Buyer Protection. Use Goods and Services for an eligible purchase and report scam payments promptly.
hero: PayPal says using Friends and Family for a purchase is a scam warning sign and those payments are not eligible for Buyer Protection.
content:
## What makes Friends and Family payments a scammer's favourite target

PayPal's Friends and Family feature is designed for sending money to people you trust — family members, close friends, or people you know personally. Unlike standard PayPal payments or goods-and-services transactions, Friends and Family transfers come with almost no buyer protection. Once you send money this way, PayPal treats it as a personal gift, not a commercial transaction. This is exactly why scammers push you towards it. They know that if you realise you've been tricked, you have almost no recourse through PayPal's dispute system. The scam works because it exploits the trust implied by the payment method itself. Scammers either impersonate someone you know — a friend, family member, or colleague — or they pose as a seller (often on Gumtree, Facebook Marketplace, or eBay) and convince you that Friends and Family is the 'safer' or 'faster' way to pay. In reality, it's the safest way for them to steal from you.

## Red flags that should stop you sending money via Friends and Family

- A seller on Gumtree, Facebook Marketplace, or eBay insists you pay via Friends and Family instead of the platform's own payment system — legitimate sellers use the built-in protection.
- Someone claiming to be a friend or family member asks for money urgently via PayPal, but their message tone, language, or phrasing feels slightly off — scammers often impersonate people via hacked accounts or spoofed messages.
- A 'buyer' for something you're selling asks to pay via Friends and Family first, then claims the money didn't arrive and asks you to send it again — a common double-payment trick.
- You receive a message from PayPal itself asking you to confirm a Friends and Family payment or verify your account — PayPal does not ask this via unsolicited messages.
- Someone you don't know well asks you to act as a 'middleman' and receive money on their behalf via Friends and Family, then forward it elsewhere — this is often money laundering or a scam setup.
- A seller offers an unusually large discount if you pay via Friends and Family instead of their normal payment method — they're trying to bypass protection systems.
- The person claims Friends and Family is 'safer' for you as a buyer — it is the opposite.

## How the scam unfolds: from contact to money loss

The scam typically begins in one of two ways. First, a scammer may hack or impersonate a real contact — a friend, family member, or colleague — and message you via WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, email, or text claiming they need money urgently. They might say they're stuck abroad, in a car accident, or facing a financial emergency. The message often has a slight oddness to it (wrong name spelling, unusual phrasing, or a request to keep it quiet), but the urgency and emotional appeal override caution. Alternatively, you may be selling something online (a phone, furniture, a car part) and a 'buyer' contacts you. They seem keen, ask for your PayPal address, and request that you send them an invoice via Friends and Family so they can 'pay quickly'. Once you do, they send you a fake PayPal email or screenshot showing the payment has been made — but it hasn't. By the time you realise the money never arrived, they've disappeared. In the impersonation version, you send the money thinking you're helping someone you trust, only to discover later (when you contact them directly) that they never asked for it. The scammer has already withdrawn or transferred the funds.

## How to check if a PayPal Friends and Family request is genuine

If someone claiming to be a friend or family member asks for money via PayPal, do not rely on the message alone. Contact them directly using a phone number or email address you already have — not one provided in the suspicious message. Call them, video call them, or message them on a platform you know is theirs (not a newly created account). Ask them directly if they sent the PayPal request. If they didn't, you've caught a scam. If you're being asked to pay a seller via Friends and Family, refuse. Legitimate sellers on Gumtree, Facebook Marketplace, eBay, and other platforms use their own payment systems or bank transfers with clear protections. If a seller insists on Friends and Family, they are either a scammer or trying to avoid accountability — either way, do not proceed. Check the PayPal email address or username of whoever is requesting the payment. Scammers often use addresses that look similar to real ones (e.g., 'paypa1' instead of 'paypal', or a name spelled slightly differently). If you're unsure, log into your own PayPal account directly (do not click links in messages) and check your recent activity or contacts. A genuine friend or family member will be someone you recognise in your PayPal contacts list.

## What to do immediately if you've already sent money

Act fast. First, log into your PayPal account and check the transaction status. If the money is still pending (not yet claimed or withdrawn), contact PayPal immediately via the official PayPal website or app — do not use any phone number from a message or email. Explain that you sent money via Friends and Family by mistake or due to a scam. PayPal may be able to cancel the payment if it hasn't been claimed. If the money has already been withdrawn, contact your bank or card issuer straight away. Tell them you sent money via PayPal to a scammer and ask if they can reverse the transaction or freeze the recipient's account. Banks can sometimes recover funds if they act quickly, especially if the money was sent to another UK bank account. Report the scam to Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040 or online at reportfraud.police.uk. Provide as much detail as possible: the PayPal address or username of the person who received the money, the date and amount, and any messages or contact details you have. If the scammer impersonated someone you know, contact that person and let them know their identity may have been compromised — they should change their passwords and check their account security. Do not send any more money or engage further with the scammer.

## Reporting the scam in the UK

Report the scam to Report Fraud immediately on 0300 123 2040 or via reportfraud.police.uk. They handle fraud reports and can flag patterns to law enforcement. Provide the PayPal username or email address of the person who received the money, the transaction ID (visible in your PayPal account), the date, amount, and any messages or contact details. Also report the scam directly to PayPal. Log into your account, go to the Resolution Centre, and report the transaction as unauthorised or fraudulent. PayPal has a dedicated fraud team and may be able to take action against the recipient's account. If the scammer impersonated someone via email or text, forward the suspicious message to the NCSC Suspicious Email Reporting Service at report@phishing.gov.uk. If it was a text message, forward it to 7726 (free, and your phone will confirm receipt). If you have contact details for the scammer (phone number, email, social media profile), report them to the platform they used — Facebook, WhatsApp, Gumtree, or eBay — so their account can be investigated and removed. Finally, contact Citizens Advice on 0808 223 1133 if you need support or guidance on next steps, especially if you've lost a significant amount of money.
sections: What the scam looks like

A seller asks the buyer to choose PayPal’s Friends and Family payment type for goods or services, often offering a discount or saying it avoids fees. The item then does not arrive or is worthless, and the buyer discovers the payment is outside PayPal Buyer Protection.
What PayPal currently says

PayPal UK says eligible Goods and Services payments can receive Buyer Protection. Its help pages list Friends and Family payments among transactions that are not eligible and describe a seller insisting on that method as a scam red flag.

PayPal’s current scam-reporting page specifically describes item-not-received and low-value-item scams in which a fraudster persuades the buyer to use Friends and Family.
When Friends and Family is appropriate

Use it only for genuine personal transfers to someone you know and trust, such as sharing a bill or sending a gift where no purchase is taking place. It should not be used to buy an item or service from a seller.
If you already paid

Report the payment promptly through PayPal’s Resolution Centre using the scam-payment route if available for the transaction. Do not falsely describe an authorised payment as “unauthorised”; explain exactly how the scam worked.

PayPal states that a PayPal-to-PayPal Friends and Family payment is not entitled to reimbursement under its APP Fraud Rules or Buyer Protection Programme. If the payment was funded by a linked card, you can ask the card issuer whether a chargeback is available, but PayPal’s role and the type of transaction can affect the outcome. Do not promise recovery.

If money was lost through fraud, report at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland; in Scotland, call Police Scotland on 101.
faq: Is a Friends and Family purchase covered by PayPal Buyer Protection?
No. PayPal UK lists Friends and Family payments as ineligible.
Is Goods and Services protection automatic for every purchase?
No. The transaction and item must be eligible, the account must meet PayPal’s conditions, and the dispute must be filed in time.
Can my card issuer reverse a linked-card payment?
Possibly, under card-scheme rules, but the issuer must assess the transaction and PayPal’s role. It is not guaranteed.

title: Printer Support Scam UK: Spot a Fake HP Contact
excerpt: Scammers pose as printer manufacturers to trick you into paying for fake repairs or handing over remote access. Learn how to spot and stop them.
description: An unsolicited caller or pop-up claims a printer fault and asks for remote access or payment. HP says it does not provide unsolicited technical support.
hero: HP says it never contacts customers to provide unsolicited technical support. End the contact and open HP Support yourself.
content:
## What is a printer support scam?

A printer support scam is a fraud where criminals pretend to be technical support staff from a printer manufacturer (such as HP, Canon, Epson, or Brother) to trick you into paying for fake repairs or giving them access to your computer. The scam typically starts with a pop-up warning on your screen, a cold call, or an email claiming your printer has a critical error, security issue, or needs urgent maintenance. The scammer's goal is to either charge you money for a 'repair' that never happens, steal your bank details or passwords, or install malware on your device that lets them access your files, photos, or financial information. These scams are growing in frequency because printers are common household devices that many people don't monitor closely, and the technical nature of the problem makes it easy to sound convincing. The scammers rely on urgency and fear — they want you to act quickly without thinking or checking whether the warning is real.

## How to spot the warning signs

- **Unsolicited pop-up warnings on your screen** — A sudden full-screen message claiming your printer is broken, has a virus, or needs immediate repair. Genuine printer manufacturers do not send pop-ups to warn you of problems; they send emails or letters to your registered account.
- **Cold calls claiming to be from printer support** — Someone rings you out of the blue saying they've detected a fault with your printer and need remote access to fix it. Real manufacturers do not cold-call customers about printer issues.
- **Emails with urgent language and suspicious links** — Messages claiming your printer warranty is expiring, your device is at risk, or you need to 'verify your account' immediately. Check the sender's email address carefully — scammers often use addresses that look similar to the real brand but have slight misspellings.
- **Requests for payment via gift cards, wire transfer, or cryptocurrency** — Legitimate printer support may charge a fee, but they use standard payment methods (credit card, debit card, invoice). Requests for iTunes cards, Google Play cards, or bank transfers are almost always a scam.
- **Pressure to grant remote access to your computer** — The caller or pop-up insists you download software or allow them to control your screen to 'diagnose' the problem. This is a major red flag; legitimate support may ask for remote access, but only after you have initiated contact with them directly.
- **Poor spelling, grammar, or awkward phrasing** — Scam emails and pop-ups often contain obvious errors. Real manufacturers employ professional communications teams.
- **A phone number that doesn't match the official website** — If you call the number provided in the pop-up or email, it doesn't connect to the real manufacturer's support line. Always use the number on your printer's documentation or the official website.
- **Requests for personal information beyond what's needed** — Asking for your full bank details, passwords, or social security number when they only need your printer model and serial number is a warning sign.

## How the scam unfolds from first contact to loss

The scam typically begins when you see a pop-up warning while browsing the internet, or you receive an unsolicited phone call or email. The pop-up might claim your printer has detected a virus, is running out of storage, or has a critical hardware error — it often includes a fake countdown timer to create panic. If you click on the pop-up or call the number provided, you reach a scammer posing as technical support. They will ask you to describe the problem (which you may not have noticed before the pop-up), then offer to fix it remotely. To do this, they ask you to download software or visit a website where you can grant them remote access to your computer. Once they have access, they may install malware, steal passwords from your browser, or take screenshots of your banking apps and login details. Alternatively, they may simply claim the 'repair' costs £50 to £300 and ask you to pay via bank transfer, gift card, or online payment. Some scammers will also try to sell you a fake 'extended warranty' or 'antivirus subscription' that you'll be charged for repeatedly. By the time you realise the printer was never broken and the support was fake, the scammer has either taken your money, installed hidden software on your device, or stolen your personal information.

## How to verify if a printer support contact is genuine

If you receive a pop-up, email, or call claiming to be from your printer manufacturer, do not click any links or call any numbers provided in the message. Instead, take these steps: First, check your printer itself — does it actually show any error messages or signs of a problem? If not, the warning is almost certainly fake. Second, go directly to the manufacturer's official website by typing the URL into your browser (do not click a link from the pop-up or email). Look for a 'Support' or 'Contact Us' section and find their official phone number or live chat. Call or message them using that contact method and ask whether they have any record of an issue with your device. Third, check your printer's documentation or the box it came in for the manufacturer's support contact details. Fourth, if you have an account with the manufacturer (for example, an HP account or Canon account), log in directly to your account on their official website and check for any notifications or alerts about your printer — scammers cannot send messages through your real account. Genuine manufacturers will never ask you to download software from a link in an unsolicited message, and they will never ask for payment via gift card or wire transfer. If you are unsure, contact Citizens Advice on 0808 223 1133 or the NCSC for guidance.

## What to do immediately if you have already engaged with the scam

If you have already interacted with a printer support scammer, act quickly in this order: First, if you granted them remote access to your computer, disconnect it from the internet immediately and do not use it until you have taken further steps. Second, if you provided your bank details, passwords, or personal information, contact your bank right away using the number on the back of your card or the official website — do not use a number from any message you received. Tell them you may have been scammed and ask them to monitor your account for suspicious activity and consider freezing it temporarily. Third, change your passwords for any important accounts (email, online banking, social media) using a different device if possible, and use a strong, unique password for each. Fourth, run a full antivirus scan on your computer using reputable software such as Windows Defender (built into Windows) or Malwarebytes. If you downloaded any software from the scammer, uninstall it immediately. Fifth, if you paid money, report it to your bank and ask about a chargeback or reversal — you may be able to recover the funds if you act quickly. Finally, report the scam to Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040 and to the NCSC if you received a phishing email.

## How to report printer support scams in the UK

Report the scam through multiple channels to help protect others and aid law enforcement. Contact Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040 (Monday to Friday, 8am to 8pm) — they handle all types of fraud and will record your report. If you received a phishing email, forward it to the NCSC Suspicious Email Reporting Service at report@phishing.gov.uk; they will investigate and work to take down the scam website. If you received a text message with a suspicious link, forward it to 7726 (spells 'SPAM') — your mobile network will investigate. If you were cold-called, you can report it to Ofcom, the communications regulator, through their website. If you paid money and your bank has not already been notified, tell them immediately so they can flag the transaction and potentially reverse it. You can also report the scam to Citizens Advice on 0808 223 1133 — they maintain a scam database and can advise you on next steps. Keep records of all communications (screenshots of pop-ups, emails, call logs, payment confirmations) as evidence for your report.
sections: What the scam looks like

A caller, email or browser page impersonates HP or another printer company and claims a fault, infection, expired driver or urgent support problem. It then seeks payment, credentials, or remote access to the computer.
What HP says

HP’s fraud alert says it never contacts customers to provide unsolicited technical support. It warns that scammers may spoof caller ID, request remote access, seek gift-card or card payment, or ask the user to install software.
Warning signs

- An unexpected call or message claiming an urgent printer problem.
- A browser warning with a phone number to call.
- A request for remote control, passwords, gift cards or unusual payment.
- A caller who prevents independent verification or becomes aggressive.
- A support site reached through an advert rather than through the manufacturer’s site.
Verify support independently

Open `support.hp.com/gb-en/contact` yourself and identify the product to see available support options. Some contact routes require an active warranty. Do not use a number shown in a pop-up or supplied by an unsolicited caller.

Close a suspicious browser tab or window without using buttons inside the page. If it will not close, use the operating system’s normal application controls and then reopen the browser without restoring the suspicious page.
If remote access or payment was given

End the session, disconnect the device from the network and contact the bank immediately from a different device if payment or banking was exposed. HP advises changing affected account passwords and running a security scan. Remove remote-access software and check for persistent access or other installed programs.

Report fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland; in Scotland, call Police Scotland on 101.
faq: Does HP make unsolicited support calls?
HP’s published fraud guidance says no.
Where is the official UK support page?
`support.hp.com/gb-en/contact`.

title: ISP Impersonation Scams UK: BT, Sky, Virgin Media and Openreach Calls
excerpt: ISP scams impersonate your internet provider to steal passwords, remote access, or payment details. Learn how to spot them and stay safe.
description: Scammers impersonate UK broadband providers or Openreach, then ask for remote access, payment or security details. How to check safely.
hero: An unexpected broadband-support call is not a reason to install remote-access software or disclose banking information.
content:
## What is an ISP scam and who is being targeted

An ISP scam is when a fraudster impersonates your internet service provider — such as BT, Virgin Media, Sky, TalkTalk, or Plusnet — to trick you into revealing sensitive information or giving them remote access to your computer. The scammer typically claims there is a fault on your line, suspicious activity on your account, or an exclusive offer available. They may say your broadband will be disconnected unless you act immediately, or that you are owed a refund. The goal is to obtain your login credentials, bank details, or permission to install remote-access software so they can steal money or personal data. These scams target a broad range of people, but are particularly effective against older adults and those less familiar with technology. The scammers rely on the fact that most people trust their ISP and are worried about losing internet access or being overcharged.

## How to recognise the warning signs of an ISP scam

- Your ISP is calling you unexpectedly about a problem you did not report — genuine providers rarely cold-call about faults unless you have already contacted them.
- The caller asks you to open a web browser and visit a specific website or enter your account details — real ISPs will never ask you to do this during an unsolicited call.
- They pressure you to act immediately or threaten disconnection — scammers create urgency to stop you thinking clearly.
- The caller asks for your full password, PIN, or security questions — your ISP already has your account details and will never ask for these over the phone.
- They offer to install remote-access software or ask you to press specific keys to "diagnose" your connection — this is a classic way to gain control of your computer.
- The number shown on your caller ID looks similar to your ISP's real number but is slightly different — scammers spoof numbers to appear legitimate.
- They ask you to pay by gift card, bank transfer, or cryptocurrency — genuine ISPs accept payment through normal billing methods only.
- The caller cannot answer basic questions about your account or uses vague technical language — real support staff will know your account details and speak clearly.

## How the scam unfolds from first contact to theft

The scam typically begins with a phone call or text message claiming to be from your ISP. The caller may say there is unusual activity on your account, a billing error, or a network fault affecting your area. They will ask you to verify your identity by providing your account number, postcode, or other personal details — information that sounds routine but is actually being collected for fraud. Once they have established a sense of trust, they escalate the request: they may ask you to visit a fake website that looks identical to your real ISP's login page, where you enter your username and password. Alternatively, they may ask you to allow them remote access to your computer by downloading software or pressing keys to open a remote-access tool. Once they have access, they can see your screen, access your email, banking apps, and stored passwords. They may then transfer money from your account, change your email password to lock you out, or steal identity information. Some scammers also use the remote access to install malware that continues stealing data long after the call ends. The entire process can take minutes, and by the time you realise what has happened, the money or data is already gone.

## How to verify if a call or message is genuinely from your ISP

If you receive an unexpected call or message claiming to be from your ISP, do not provide any information or click any links. Instead, hang up or delete the message and contact your ISP directly using the number on your bill or the official website. Never use a number provided by the caller, as scammers often give you a fake support line that they control. When you call your ISP's genuine number, ask them directly whether they have tried to contact you about the issue mentioned. Real ISPs will have a record of any legitimate contact attempts. Check your account online by logging in through the official website or app — if there is a genuine problem, it will be visible there. Your ISP will never ask you to visit a website during an unsolicited call, and they will never ask for your full password or PIN. If you are unsure whether a website is real, type the ISP's name directly into your browser rather than clicking a link from the call or message. Look for the padlock icon and "https" in the address bar, and check that the domain name is spelled correctly — scammers often use URLs that are very similar to the real one but with a subtle misspelling.

## What to do immediately if you have already engaged with the scammer

If you have given remote access to your computer, disconnect it from the internet immediately and do not use it until you have taken action. If you provided your ISP password, log into your account from another device and change your password to something completely new. If you gave your bank details or made a payment, contact your bank right away on the number on the back of your card or the official website — do not use a number the scammer provided. Ask your bank to freeze your account and watch for unauthorised transactions. If you transferred money via bank transfer or paid by gift card, report it to your bank and the police as soon as possible; there is a small chance the money can be recovered if reported quickly. If you installed any software the scammer asked you to, consider running a full antivirus scan using reputable software such as Windows Defender (built into Windows) or Malwarebytes. If you are not confident doing this yourself, take your computer to a local IT repair shop. Change the passwords for your email, online banking, and any other important accounts, as the scammer may have access to them. Do not delay — the longer you wait, the more damage they can do.

## How to report an ISP scam in the UK

Report the scam to Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040 or online at reportfraud.police.uk. They will log the details and may be able to trace the scammer's bank account if money was transferred. If you received a suspicious text message, forward it to 7726 (spamming) — this alerts your mobile network to the scam. If the scam involved a phishing email or fake website, report it to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) by emailing report@phishing.gov.uk with details of the website URL and any emails involved. You can also report the scam to Citizens Advice on 0808 223 1133; they keep records of scam patterns and can advise you on next steps. If money was stolen, also report it to your local police force via their online reporting tool or by calling 101 (non-emergency). Keep a record of all communications — screenshots of texts, the phone number that called you, the date and time, and any website URLs — as this information will be needed by investigators. The more people who report the same scammer, the faster action can be taken.
sections: What the scam looks like

An unsolicited caller claims to be from BT, Sky, Virgin Media, Openreach or a technical partner. They may mention a fault, slow broadband, suspicious activity, a router problem or the Digital Voice transition, then ask you to install software, visit a link, share a password or make a payment.

The caller may know your name, address or provider. That information does not authenticate the call, and caller ID can be spoofed. The genuine software named by the caller may be a legitimate remote-support product; the danger is granting access because an unexpected caller tells you to.
Warning signs

- An unexpected call creates an urgent fault or disconnection story.
- The caller asks for remote access to a computer, router or phone.
- You are asked for a banking password, PIN, one-time code or card details.
- You are told to pay an unexpected fee or to move money to protect an account.
- The caller discourages you from hanging up or checking with the provider.
- A link or phone number is supplied instead of asking you to use the provider’s official contact route.

The UK’s landline migration is real, but a real programme does not make an unexpected caller genuine. Check any Digital Voice information directly with your provider using a number or account you already trust.
How to respond

Hang up and contact your provider through its official website, app, bill or the number on your contract. Do not use a number supplied by the caller. Never install remote-access software or share security credentials because of an unsolicited call.

If you installed software, disconnect the affected device from the internet and seek help removing it. Contact your bank immediately if the caller saw banking information, codes or a payment was made. Keep the caller’s number, messages, websites and payment details as evidence.

Forward suspicious texts to 7726. Report fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland; in Scotland, call Police Scotland on 101. Report an unlicensed or misleading communications service to the relevant provider or regulator where appropriate.
faq: Will a genuine provider ever contact me about a fault?

Providers can contact customers, so the subject of a call is not enough to authenticate it. If the caller asks for remote access, passwords, banking details, codes or an unexpected payment, hang up and verify through the provider’s official route.
Is TeamViewer or AnyDesk itself a scam?
No. These are legitimate tools, but an unexpected caller who asks you to install or open them is a serious warning sign.
Do I need to pay for the Digital Voice transition?

Do not pay an unexpected caller. The transition and any equipment or plan changes should be confirmed through your provider’s official account or support channel, because arrangements differ between providers and customers.
I gave a caller remote access. What should I do?

Disconnect the device, contact your bank if financial information may have been exposed, change passwords from a clean device, and get trusted technical help before reconnecting it. Report the incident and preserve evidence.

title: Microsoft Account Suspended Scam Email: How to Spot It
excerpt: Scammers send fake Microsoft account suspension emails to steal passwords and personal data. Learn how to spot them and what to do if you've clicked.
description: A fake Microsoft email claims unusual activity or suspension and links to a bogus sign-in page. Open your Microsoft account directly instead.
hero: Microsoft gives `micros0ft.com`, with a zero replacing the second “o”, as an example of a lookalike domain used in phishing.
content:
## What this scam looks like

The Microsoft account suspended email scam is a phishing attack where criminals send emails that appear to come from Microsoft, claiming your account has been locked, suspended, or flagged for suspicious activity. The email typically says you need to verify your identity, confirm your password, or update your payment details urgently — often within 24 hours. The message creates a false sense of panic by suggesting your account will be permanently closed or your data will be deleted unless you act immediately. The email includes a button or link that looks like it goes to Microsoft's official login page, but actually leads to a fake website controlled by the scammer. Once you enter your Microsoft account credentials, recovery email, or payment information on that fake page, the scammer has everything they need to access your real account, steal your data, or commit fraud in your name.

## Red flags that give away the fake email

- The sender's email address does not match Microsoft's official domain (microsoft.com). Look carefully — scammers use addresses like microsoftaccount-verify@gmail.com or support@microsoft-security.net that look similar but are not genuine.
- The email asks you to click a link and log in, or to reply with your password or personal details. Microsoft never asks for passwords via email.
- The message uses generic greetings like "Dear User" or "Dear Customer" instead of your actual name, which Microsoft systems typically include.
- The email contains spelling, grammar, or formatting errors, or uses awkward phrasing that does not match Microsoft's professional tone.
- Urgent language and artificial deadlines ("verify within 24 hours" or "your account will be closed") are designed to panic you into acting without thinking.
- The link in the email does not go to a Microsoft domain when you hover over it (on desktop, move your mouse over the link without clicking to see the real URL).
- The email arrived unexpectedly and you have not recently changed your account settings, made a suspicious login attempt, or requested a password reset.

## How the scam unfolds from the first email

The scam begins when you receive an email that appears to come from Microsoft, with a subject line designed to alarm you — such as "Your account has been suspended" or "Urgent: Verify your Microsoft account now." The email body explains that your account has been locked due to suspicious activity, an unrecognised login, or a security concern, and instructs you to click a link to verify your identity or confirm your details. When you click the link, you are taken to a fake Microsoft login page that looks almost identical to the real one. If you enter your email address and password, the scammer captures both. Some fake pages then ask for additional information, such as your recovery email address, phone number, or payment card details, claiming this is needed to "unlock" your account. Once the scammer has your credentials, they can log into your real Microsoft account, access your emails, OneDrive files, and linked services like Outlook. They may also use your account to send phishing emails to your contacts, reset your password to lock you out, or use your payment details to make purchases or subscriptions.

## How to check if a Microsoft email is genuine

If you receive an email claiming to be from Microsoft, do not click any links in the email. Instead, open your web browser and go directly to account.microsoft.com by typing the address yourself, or use the Microsoft Authenticator app if you have it installed. Log in with your credentials and check your account status — if there are any genuine security alerts, they will appear in your account dashboard, not just in an email. You can also check your recent activity and login history to see if there has been any suspicious access. If you are unsure whether an email is real, contact Microsoft directly by visiting their official support website (support.microsoft.com) and using their contact options there — never use a phone number or email address from the suspicious email itself. Microsoft's official emails will always come from an address ending in @microsoft.com, and they will never ask you to verify your password or payment details by clicking a link in an email. If the email claims your account is suspended, log in to your account directly to verify — a genuine suspension would be visible in your account settings, not just announced in an email.

## What to do immediately if you have already clicked or entered details

If you clicked the link but did not enter any information, you are likely safe — simply delete the email and move on. If you entered your Microsoft password on the fake page, change your password immediately by logging into your real Microsoft account at account.microsoft.com. Use a strong, unique password that you have not used anywhere else. If you also entered your recovery email address or phone number, update those in your account settings to ensure the scammer cannot use them to reset your password. If you entered payment card details, contact your bank or card issuer right away to report the incident and ask them to monitor your account for fraudulent transactions; they may issue you a new card as a precaution. Check your account's recent activity and login history to see if anyone else has accessed it since you entered your details. If you see unfamiliar logins or activity, change your password again and enable two-factor authentication (also called multi-factor authentication) on your Microsoft account to add an extra layer of security. If you have linked services such as Outlook, OneDrive, or Xbox to your Microsoft account, check those services for any unauthorised changes or activity as well.

## Reporting the scam in the UK

Report the phishing email to the NCSC Suspicious Email Reporting Service by forwarding it to report@phishing.gov.uk. Include the full email header if possible (most email clients have an option to view the original message or source code). You can also report the scam to Report Fraud by calling 0300 123 2040 or visiting their website — they handle fraud and scams across the UK and pass information to law enforcement and banks. If you have lost money or believe your account has been compromised, contact Citizens Advice consumer helpline on 0808 223 1133 for guidance on next steps and your rights. Report the fake website (if you noted the URL) to the NCSC as well, as they work to take down phishing pages. If the scammer has accessed your Microsoft account and sent emails from it to your contacts, consider notifying your contacts that your account may have been compromised so they do not fall for similar emails sent in your name. Keep a record of all emails, screenshots, and the date and time you received the message — this information is useful if you need to make a formal complaint or claim.
sections: What the scam looks like

The email claims unusual sign-in activity, a security hold or an imminent suspension affecting a Microsoft, Outlook or Xbox account. It creates urgency and links to a page made to resemble a Microsoft sign-in. A fraudulent page may steal the credentials entered into it. A phone call or pop-up claiming to be Microsoft technical support is a different pattern; see /guides/microsoft-support-scam-uk-guide/.
Microsoft's published warning signs

Microsoft advises users to watch for urgent demands, unexpected senders, generic greetings, poor spelling or grammar, mismatched links and lookalike domains. Its examples include `micros0ft.com` and `rnicrosoft.com`. None of those signs is conclusive on its own, and polished phishing emails may contain no language errors.
Outlook indicators

Outlook may show a question-mark icon for an unverified sender, an underlined “via” label when the visible From address differs from the authenticated sending domain, or a warning that it could not verify the sender. Microsoft cautions that not every unverified message or “via” label is malicious.
Check the account safely

Do not use the email link. Open a new tab and type `account.microsoft.com`, then review security and recent activity. Microsoft says that if an unusual-activity email is uncertain, you can safely sign in directly without clicking the email.
If credentials were entered

Use Microsoft's compromised-account guidance. Scan the affected computer for malware, change or reset the password, review recent activity and account settings, and enable two-step verification. Change the password on other accounts if it was reused. For a work or school account, notify the organisation's IT administrator as well.
Report the phishing email

In Microsoft 365 Outlook or Outlook.com, select the message and choose `Report > Report phishing`. Microsoft no longer publishes a general mailbox for forwarding phishing emails from other email clients; a work or school account holder can instead use the Submissions page in the Microsoft Defender portal, and anyone else should forward the email to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk`.

If money was lost or an account was hacked, report the crime to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland; in Scotland, call Police Scotland on 101.
faq: Where should I check a claimed suspension?
Go directly to `account.microsoft.com`; do not follow the email link.
Does an Outlook warning prove the email is malicious?
No. It is a reason for caution, not proof. Verify the claim by signing in directly.

title: Is AliExpress a Scam? UK Guide to Marketplace Risk
excerpt: AliExpress scams use fake websites and phishing emails to steal payment details and personal data from UK shoppers. Learn how to spot them and stay safe.
description: AliExpress is an Alibaba marketplace, but listings and sellers vary. Keep payment on-platform and use the dispute or return deadline shown on the order.
hero: AliExpress is an Alibaba Group retail marketplace; that does not make every third-party listing genuine or every purchase protected in the same way.
content:
## What is the AliExpress scam?

The AliExpress scam comes in two main forms. First, scammers create fake AliExpress websites that look almost identical to the real one — same logo, layout, and product listings — but are designed to capture your payment card details, address, and login credentials when you try to buy something. Second, you receive phishing emails or text messages claiming to be from AliExpress, asking you to 'verify your account', 'confirm your payment method', or 'claim a refund'. These messages contain links to fake login pages or payment forms. The real AliExpress is a Chinese-owned online marketplace that operates legitimately in the UK, but its popularity makes it an attractive target for scammers. The fake sites and messages are so convincing that many UK shoppers don't realise they've been targeted until they see unauthorised charges on their bank statement or their account is compromised.

## Warning signs of a fake AliExpress site or message

- The website URL does not match the official AliExpress domain — check the address bar carefully; scammers use similar-looking URLs like 'aliexpress-uk.com' or 'aliexpress.co.uk' instead of the real domain.
- The site asks you to log in or enter payment details before you've added anything to your basket — the real AliExpress does not do this.
- The email or text claims there is an urgent problem with your account, a pending refund, or a security issue requiring immediate action — this is a classic phishing tactic.
- The message contains spelling mistakes, awkward phrasing, or poor grammar — AliExpress communications are professionally written.
- You are asked to click a link in an email or text to 'verify' or 'confirm' anything — AliExpress will never ask you to do this via email or SMS.
- The website looks slightly off — colours are wrong, buttons are in odd places, or images are blurry or misaligned.
- The site offers unrealistic discounts or claims you have won a prize you never entered — this is bait to get you to enter your details.
- Payment options are limited to bank transfer or cryptocurrency only — the real AliExpress accepts major credit and debit cards.

## How the scam works from start to finish

The scam typically begins when you receive an email or text message that appears to come from AliExpress. The message might say your account has been locked, a payment has failed, or you are eligible for a refund. It includes a link that takes you to a fake website that mimics the real AliExpress so closely that most people don't notice the difference. When you click the link and enter your login details, the scammers capture them immediately. If the fake site asks for payment information, you may enter your card details thinking you are completing a legitimate purchase or confirming a refund. Some scammers go further and create fake checkout pages that look identical to the real thing, complete with a fake order confirmation email sent to you afterwards. By the time you realise something is wrong — either because you see charges on your bank statement, your real AliExpress account is compromised, or you never receive the item you thought you bought — the scammers have already used your details to make fraudulent purchases, sell your information to other criminals, or drain your account.

## How to verify you are on the real AliExpress website

Before you enter any personal or payment information, take these steps to confirm you are on the genuine AliExpress site. First, check the URL in the address bar — it must be 'www.aliexpress.com' or 'www.aliexpress.co.uk' (the UK version). Do not rely on what the page says; look at the actual web address. Second, if you received an email or text with a link, do not click it. Instead, open your web browser, type the AliExpress URL directly into the address bar, and log in from there. Third, look for the padlock icon next to the URL — this indicates the site uses encryption, though this alone does not guarantee it is safe. Fourth, check the site's security certificate by clicking the padlock; it should show the certificate is issued to AliExpress. Fifth, if you are logging in, use a strong, unique password that you do not use anywhere else. If you are ever unsure, contact AliExpress directly through their official website or app before entering any details. The real AliExpress will never ask you to verify your account via email or text message.

## What to do if you have already entered your details

Act quickly if you believe you have been caught by an AliExpress scam. First, if you entered your card details on a fake site, contact your bank immediately — use the number on the back of your card or the official number on your bank's website, never a number from the scam message. Ask your bank to cancel your card and watch for unauthorised transactions. Second, if you entered your AliExpress login details, change your password immediately by logging into the real AliExpress website (not via any link in an email). Use a strong, unique password. Third, check your real AliExpress account for any orders you did not make and cancel them if possible. Fourth, if you paid money directly to the scammers via bank transfer or cryptocurrency, contact your bank straight away — recovery is difficult but not impossible if you act within hours. Fifth, monitor your bank statements and credit reports for the next few months for any suspicious activity. If you see unauthorised charges, report them to your bank and ask them to dispute the transactions. Sixth, report the scam to Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040 and to the NCSC if you received a phishing email.

## How to report an AliExpress scam in the UK

Report the scam through multiple channels to help protect other UK shoppers and aid law enforcement. First, contact Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040 — this is the UK's national fraud reporting service and they will log your report and advise you on next steps. Second, if you received a phishing email, forward it to the NCSC Suspicious Email Reporting Service at report@phishing.gov.uk — include the full email header if possible. Third, if you received a phishing text message, forward it to 7726 (spells 'SPAM') — your mobile network will investigate. Fourth, report the fake website to the real AliExpress by contacting their customer service through the official website or app; they can take action to shut down the fake site. Fifth, if you have lost money, report it to your bank's fraud team and ask them to file a report with the Financial Conduct Authority if appropriate. Sixth, you can also contact Citizens Advice on 0808 223 1133 for guidance on your consumer rights and next steps. Keep records of all communications, screenshots of the fake site, and copies of any messages you received — these will help with your report and any potential recovery.
sections: What is verified about the platform

Alibaba Group says AliExpress launched in 2010 as a global retail e-commerce platform that connects consumers with manufacturers and merchants. It is therefore inaccurate to describe the whole platform as a fabricated site.

Buyers can still encounter goods that do not arrive, do not match the listing, are unsafe or infringe intellectual-property rights. Assess the individual seller, listing and protection terms.
Warning signs

- A price that is implausibly low for the claimed brand or specification.
- A seller with little history or reviews that do not discuss the actual product.
- Stock images with no useful buyer evidence.
- A request to pay, communicate or accept a refund outside AliExpress.
- Pressure to confirm receipt before inspection.
Buyer Protection and Free Return are not one universal promise

AliExpress's 15-calendar-day Free Return window applies only to products carrying the `Free Return` label. It is a particular programme with its own eligibility and return-condition rules — not a universal 15-day guarantee for every order. Check the specific deadline shown on your own order rather than assuming the same window applies to non-delivery, damage or misdescription claims generally.

For a problem, open the order in the AliExpress account and use the dispute or return control before the deadline displayed there. Save screenshots of the listing, seller messages, tracking and the condition of the item.

Refund processing times vary by payment method and dispute type, so check the timeframe given for your specific case rather than assuming a fixed number of working days.
UK card protection

Chargeback may apply under card-scheme rules, commonly with a time limit around 120 days. Section 75 may apply to a qualifying credit-card purchase where the cash price is over £100 and not more than £30,000, but a marketplace or payment intermediary can affect the required debtor-creditor-supplier relationship. Ask the issuer to assess the claim.
Reporting

Use the order’s dispute process and AliExpress Help Centre. If the issue is fraud and money was lost, report at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland; in Scotland, call Police Scotland on 101. Unsafe products can also be reported to Citizens Advice for referral to Trading Standards.
faq: Is AliExpress owned by Alibaba Group?
Yes. Alibaba Group identifies AliExpress as one of its e-commerce businesses.
Does every AliExpress order have the same 15-day protection window?
No. Fifteen days applies specifically to eligible `Free Return` products; other dispute rights and deadlines depend on the specific order.
Is section 75 automatic on AliExpress?
No. The cash-price and credit requirements matter, and the marketplace/payment structure may affect the claim.

title: PayPal Account Limited Email Scam UK
excerpt: Scammers impersonate PayPal to trick you into confirming account details. Learn how to spot the fake email and protect your money.
description: An email says your PayPal account is limited and you must verify now? Log in directly instead. Genuine emails use your account name.
hero: A genuine PayPal email addresses you by the full name listed on your account, not 'Dear PayPal user'.
content:
## What this PayPal scam actually is

This is a phishing scam where criminals send an email that looks like it comes from PayPal, claiming your account has been limited, restricted, or flagged for suspicious activity. The email creates a false sense of urgency — saying you must act immediately to avoid losing access to your money. It includes a button or link that appears to take you to PayPal, but actually leads to a fake website controlled by the scammers. When you enter your login details on that fake site, the criminals capture your email address, password, and any payment card information you enter. They can then access your real PayPal account, steal money, make unauthorised purchases, or use your details to commit fraud elsewhere. The scam works because PayPal is a trusted brand that handles real money, so people are more likely to panic and click without thinking carefully.

## Red flags that give away the fake PayPal email

- The sender's email address does not match PayPal's official domain. Real PayPal emails come from addresses ending in @paypal.com or @service.paypal.com — anything else is a red flag.
- The email uses generic greetings like 'Dear Customer' or 'Dear User' instead of your actual name. PayPal always addresses you by your registered name.
- The message creates artificial urgency, saying your account will be closed, frozen, or limited unless you act within hours. Genuine PayPal notices give you time to respond.
- The email asks you to click a link to 'verify', 'confirm', 'update', or 'reactivate' your account. PayPal rarely asks you to click email links to log in — they ask you to go directly to the website yourself.
- The link in the email does not match the text it displays. Hover over the link (do not click) to see where it actually goes — if it points to a different website or a suspicious URL, it is fake.
- The email contains spelling, grammar, or formatting errors, or uses odd phrasing that does not match PayPal's professional tone.
- The email threatens account closure, legal action, or money loss if you do not act immediately. Real PayPal communications are firm but not threatening in this way.

## How the scam unfolds from the fake email to stolen details

The scam begins when you receive an email that appears to come from PayPal, often with a subject line like 'Your Account Has Been Limited' or 'Urgent: Verify Your Account'. The email includes a button or hyperlink that says something like 'Confirm Your Account' or 'Verify Now'. When you click it, you are taken to a website that looks almost identical to the real PayPal login page — same colours, logos, and layout. You enter your email address and password, thinking you are logging into your genuine account. The fake site then asks for additional information: your date of birth, your full address, your card number, expiry date, and security code. Some versions ask for your bank details or security questions. Once you submit this information, it is sent directly to the scammers' server, not to PayPal. They now have everything needed to access your real PayPal account, drain your balance, or use your card details to make purchases. Many victims do not realise they have been scammed until they try to log into their real PayPal account and find the password no longer works — because the scammers have already changed it.

## How to check if a PayPal email is genuine

If you receive an email claiming to be from PayPal, do not click any links in it. Instead, open your web browser and go directly to paypal.com by typing the address yourself — do not use a link from the email. Log into your account using your own password. Once logged in, check your account status and messages. If PayPal has genuinely limited your account, you will see a notification in your account dashboard, not just in an email. You can also contact PayPal directly by going to their Help Centre on the official website and using their secure messaging system. Another way to verify: check the sender's email address very carefully. Real PayPal emails come from @paypal.com or @service.paypal.com addresses only. If the email came from any other domain, it is definitely fake. You can also forward the suspicious email to the NCSC Suspicious Email Reporting Service at report@phishing.gov.uk — they will investigate and may take action against the scammers. Never reply to the email or click any links, as this confirms your email address is active and may lead to more scam attempts.

## What to do immediately if you have already clicked the link or entered details

If you clicked the link and entered your PayPal login details, change your PayPal password right now. Go to the real PayPal website (paypal.com), log in if you can, and change your password to something completely new that you have not used before. If you cannot log in because the scammers have already changed the password, use PayPal's 'Forgot Password' option to reset it. If you entered your card details on the fake site, contact your bank or card issuer immediately — use the number on the back of your card or the number on your bank statement, never a number from the email. Ask them to cancel that card and issue a replacement. Monitor your account for unauthorised transactions over the next few weeks. If you entered your bank details, contact your bank directly and tell them you may have been scammed; they can flag your account for suspicious activity. Check your PayPal account for any unauthorised transactions, linked cards, or changes to your address or phone number. If you spot anything unusual, change your password again and contact PayPal's secure help centre. Report the scam to Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040 and to the NCSC at report@phishing.gov.uk.

## How to report the PayPal scam in the UK

Report the scam through multiple channels to maximise the chance of action. First, forward the suspicious email to the NCSC Suspicious Email Reporting Service at report@phishing.gov.uk — they investigate phishing emails and work to shut down fake websites. Second, report it to Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040 or online at reportfraud.police.uk. They log scam reports and share data with law enforcement and banks. Third, report it directly to PayPal by forwarding the email to their phishing team — you can find the correct address in PayPal's Help Centre under 'Report Suspicious Emails'. Fourth, if you have lost money, contact your bank or card issuer and ask them to file a fraud report on your behalf. Keep a copy of the fake email and take screenshots of the fake website if you can access it again (do not log in). Write down the date and time you received the email, what you clicked, and what information you entered. This information helps investigators trace the scammers and may support a claim for a refund.
sections: What a fake PayPal 'account limited' email looks like

This scam is an email designed to look like it is from PayPal, claiming your account has been limited and needs urgent verification. An example of the style: `Your account has been limited due to unusual activity. Verify your details within 24 hours to restore full access.` It usually includes a link to a page built to look like PayPal's genuine login.
Why these emails are convincing
PayPal genuinely can limit accounts, so the concept itself is not unusual. The urgency and threat of losing account access pushes people to click before checking carefully.
Signs a PayPal email is a scam

- It is addressed to 'Dear PayPal user' or similar, rather than the full name listed on your account.
- It asks you to click a link and enter your card, bank, or login details.
- It creates urgency with a short deadline to 'verify' your account.
- The link, when you hover over it, does not go to paypal.com.
How the scam works step by step

First, an email claims your account is limited and needs urgent action. Second, a link opens a page built to look like PayPal's genuine login or verification screen. Third, whatever you enter - login details, card number, or bank details - is captured. Fourth, the criminal can access your real PayPal account or use the payment details elsewhere.
How to check a PayPal email is genuine

Do not click the link. Log into PayPal directly through the app or by typing paypal.com yourself, and check the Resolution Centre there for any genuine account issue.

- Genuine PayPal emails address you by the full name listed on your PayPal account, or your business name.
- If there is a real limitation on your account, it will show up when you log in directly. You do not need to act on the email itself.
If you have already entered your details
Log into PayPal directly and change your password immediately. Check your account for any transactions or changes you do not recognise, and contact your bank if you entered card or bank details.
How to report a fake PayPal email (UK)

Forward it to PayPal at `phishing@paypal.com`. If you have lost money, also report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

title: Fake Wi-Fi Hotspot Scam UK: Verify the Network
excerpt: Scammers create fake public Wi-Fi networks to steal your passwords, banking details, and personal data. Learn how to spot them and stay safe.
description: An “evil twin” copies a legitimate Wi-Fi name. Ask the venue for the correct network and prefer mobile data for sensitive activity.
hero: Ask staff for the exact network name. For sensitive work, mobile data or a trusted, correctly configured VPN reduces exposure to a rogue hotspot.
content:
## What is a fake Wi-Fi hotspot scam?

A fake Wi-Fi hotspot scam happens when a criminal sets up a wireless network with a name that looks legitimate — often mimicking the real Wi-Fi of a cafe, airport, or hotel. When you connect to it, the scammer can see everything you do online: passwords, banking logins, emails, and personal messages. They may also inject malware onto your device or redirect you to fake websites designed to steal your details. The scam is particularly dangerous because it requires no interaction from you beyond connecting — you don't need to click a link or enter credentials. The criminal simply sits nearby with a laptop or small device, passively collecting data from everyone connected to their fake network. This type of attack is sometimes called 'evil twin' Wi-Fi because it impersonates a legitimate network.

## Warning signs of a fake Wi-Fi hotspot

- No password required: Real public Wi-Fi in businesses often has no password, but if a network appears suddenly and has no security, be cautious — especially if it's identical to the venue's usual network name.
- Suspicious network name: Look for slight misspellings of the cafe or airport name, or generic names like 'Free Public Wi-Fi' or 'Airport Guest' that don't match the actual venue.
- No login page: Legitimate public Wi-Fi usually shows a login or terms-of-service page when you first connect. If you connect and nothing appears, disconnect immediately.
- Unusually slow speeds: If the network is extremely slow or keeps dropping, it may be a scammer's device with limited bandwidth.
- Network appears suddenly: If a network with the venue's name appears when it wasn't there before, ask staff which is the real one.
- Duplicate networks: If you see two networks with nearly identical names, one is likely fake — ask staff which is genuine.
- You're asked to install software: Legitimate public Wi-Fi never asks you to install apps or drivers to connect.

## How the scam works from connection to data theft

The scammer sets up a fake Wi-Fi network using a laptop, mobile hotspot, or dedicated device, usually in a busy public place where people expect free Wi-Fi. They give it a name that closely matches the real venue's network — for example, 'Costa_WiFi' instead of 'Costa Coffee Guest' — or a generic-sounding name like 'Airport Free Wi-Fi'. When you connect, your device begins sending data across the network. The scammer's device intercepts this traffic using freely available software tools. If you log into your email, online banking, or social media while connected, the scammer captures your username and password in real time. They can also see any sensitive information you type, including credit card numbers if you shop online. More sophisticated scammers may set up a fake login page that appears when you first connect, tricking you into entering your details directly. Once they have your credentials, they can access your accounts, steal money, or sell your information to other criminals. The entire process can happen without you noticing anything unusual.

## How to verify you're connecting to the real Wi-Fi

Before connecting to any public Wi-Fi, ask staff at the venue for the exact network name and whether it requires a password. Most legitimate businesses can tell you this immediately. Check the venue's website or social media — many post their Wi-Fi details online. If the network name looks slightly wrong or you're unsure, do not connect. Look for a login page: when you connect to real public Wi-Fi, your browser should automatically open a login or welcome page within a few seconds. If nothing appears, disconnect. Check for HTTPS: before entering any sensitive information, look for the padlock icon in your browser's address bar, which indicates an encrypted connection. However, do not rely on this alone — scammers can sometimes fake this too. Use your phone's hotspot instead: if you're unsure about the Wi-Fi, use your mobile data or create a personal hotspot from your phone to share with your laptop. This is always safer than public Wi-Fi. Ask other people: if you're in a cafe or airport, ask someone else nearby if they're connected to the same network and whether it's working properly.

## What to do immediately if you've connected to a fake Wi-Fi

If you suspect you've connected to a fake network, disconnect immediately and do not use that Wi-Fi again. Stop using the internet on that device until you've taken steps to secure it. Change your passwords from a different, secure network — ideally your home Wi-Fi or mobile data — starting with your email and online banking. Use a different device to change passwords if possible, so the compromised device doesn't capture your new credentials. Check your bank and credit card statements for any unauthorised transactions. If you entered banking details, credit card information, or passwords while connected, contact your bank immediately using the number on the back of your card or the official number on their website. Enable two-factor authentication on all your important accounts (email, banking, social media) if you haven't already. Run a malware scan on the device using reputable antivirus software. Consider changing your Wi-Fi password at home if you've recently connected to public networks from your home device. Monitor your credit report through Clearscore or Experian for signs of identity theft.

## Reporting a fake Wi-Fi hotspot in the UK

If you've identified a fake Wi-Fi network or believe you've been targeted by one, report it to Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040 or online at reportfraud.police.uk. Provide the network name, location, date, and time you encountered it. If you've lost money or had your bank details compromised, your bank must be notified first — they can freeze accounts and dispute fraudulent transactions. Report the incident to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) by emailing report@phishing.gov.uk if the scam involved a fake login page or phishing attempt. You can also contact Citizens Advice on 0808 223 1133 for guidance on next steps and your consumer rights. If you believe your identity has been stolen, register a Cifas Protective Registration, which flags your details to lenders and the credit reference agencies (Experian, Equifax and TransUnion) so they check more carefully before opening credit in your name. Keep records of all communications, screenshots of the network name, and any evidence of unauthorised access to your accounts. These details will help investigators and support any dispute claims with your bank.
sections: What an evil twin is

NCSC describes an evil twin as an attacker-owned access point that uses the same or a similar name as a legitimate network, potentially allowing the attacker to intercept or manipulate traffic from connected devices.

The name alone is therefore not enough. Two networks can look identical in a phone’s Wi-Fi list.
HTTPS helps, but does not validate the hotspot

Modern banking, email and shopping services normally use HTTPS/TLS to encrypt traffic between the device and the genuine service. That materially limits what a local network attacker can read or alter.

It does not make a fake hotspot harmless. An attacker can still present a deceptive captive portal, exploit unencrypted or badly configured services, probe exposed local services, or direct the user to a phishing site. A padlock proves the connection to the domain shown in the browser, not that the Wi-Fi belongs to the venue.
Warning signs

- Duplicate or near-duplicate network names.
- A captive portal asking for an email password, banking details or an unrelated account login.
- Certificate or browser security warnings.
- Staff cannot confirm the network name or access method.
- The device reconnects automatically to an unexpected open network.

An open network is not automatically fraudulent; many legitimate venues operate one. Verification matters more than whether a password is present.
Safer connection choices

Ask venue staff to identify the correct network. For sensitive activity, using your own mobile connection instead of an unknown hotspot avoids the rogue-access-point problem. If an organisation provides a trusted, properly configured full-device VPN, it can protect traffic across an untrusted local network; NCSC’s “evil twin” exercise says VPN use can prevent this interception pattern.

Do not install a random “free VPN” in response to a pop-up. A VPN operator can itself see or influence traffic and must be trusted.
If you connected to a suspicious network

Disconnect and forget the network so the device does not automatically rejoin. From a trusted connection, change any password entered into the hotspot or a suspicious page, review account sessions and enable a passkey or two-step verification. If software or a certificate profile was installed, remove it and follow the device vendor’s security guidance.

If money was lost or accounts were compromised, report at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland; in Scotland, call Police Scotland on 101.
faq: Does HTTPS remove all public Wi-Fi risk?
No. It strongly protects traffic to a correctly authenticated HTTPS service, but it does not prove the network or a captive portal is genuine.
Is every password-free hotspot fake?
No. Confirm the network with the venue rather than using the presence or absence of a password as the deciding test.
Does NCSC tell every individual to buy a VPN?

No. NCSC’s detailed VPN guidance is mainly for organisations. Its evil-twin material says a VPN can prevent that attack, while other NCSC advice recommends verifying the hotspot or using mobile tethering.
